source_text: Καὶ ὅλα δὲ, ἅπερ ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος λέγει πρὸς τοὺς πιστεύοντας εἰς τὸν Ἰησοῦν, δύναται κοινοποιεῖσθαι εἰς τὴν Μωϋσέως κατηγορίαν· ὥστ᾿ ἢ μηδὲν διαφέρειν ἢ παραπλήσιον εἶναι λέγειν γοητείαν τὴν Ἰησοῦ τῇ Μωϋσέως, ἀμφοτέρων ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ λέξει τοῦ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαίου δυναμένων τοῖς αὐτοῖς ὑπάγεσθαι ἐγκλήμασιν. οἷον περὶ μὲν Χριστοῦ ὁ παρὰ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος λέγει· ἀλλ᾿ ὦ φῶς καὶ ἀλήθεια. τῇ αὐτοῦ φωνῇ διαῤῥήδην ἐξαγορεύει Ἰησοῦς ταῦτα, καθὰ καὶ ὑμεῖς συγγεγράφατε. διότι παρέσονται ὑμῖν καὶ ἕτεροι δυνάμεσιν ὁμοίαις χρώμενοι, κακοὶ καὶ γόητες· περὶ δὲ Μωϋσέως εἴποι ἂν ὁ ἀπιστῶν πρὸς τὸν Ἰουδαῖον τοῖς Μωϋσέως εἴτ᾿ Αἰγύπτιος εἴθ᾿ ὁστισοῦν· ἀλλ᾿ ὦ φῶς καὶ ἀλήθεια, τῇ αὐτοῦ φωνῇ Μωϋσῆς διαῤῥήδην ἐξαγορεύει. καθὰ καὶ ὑμεῖς συγγεγράφατε, διότι παρέσονται ὑμῖν ἕτεροι δυνάμεσιν ὁμοίαις χρώμενοι, κακοὶ καὶ γόητες. γέγραπται γὰρ ὑμῶν ἐν τῷ νόμῳ· „ἐὰν δὲ ἀναστῇ ἐν σοὶ προφήτης ἢ ἐνυπνιαζόμενος ἐνύπνιον καὶ δῷ σοι σημεῖον ἢ τέρας, καὶ ἔλθῃ τὸ σημεῖον ἢ τὸ τέρας, ὃ ἐλάλησε πρός σε λέγων· πορευθῶμεν καὶ ἀκολουθήσωμεν θεοῖς ἑτέροις, οὓς οὐκ οἴδατε, καὶ λατρεύσωμεν αὐτοῖς. οὐκ ἀκούσεσθε τοὺς λόγους τοῦ προφήτου ἐκείνου ἢ τοῦ ἐνυπνιαζομένου τὸ ἐνύπνιον ἐκεῖνο“ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. καὶ ὁ μὲν τοὺς λόγους τοῦ Ἰησοῦ διαβάλλων φησὶ καὶ σατανᾶν τινα τοιαῦτα παραμηχανώμενον ὀνομάζειν, ὁ δὲ κοινοποιῶν τοῦτο πρὸς Μωϋσέα ἐρεῖ καὶ προφήτην ἐνυπνιαζόμενον τοιαῦτα παραμηχανώμενον ὀνομάζειν. ὥσπερ δ᾿ ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖός φησι περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ὅτι ὥστε οὐδ᾿ αὐτὸς ἔξαρνός ἐστιν, ὡς ταῦτά γε οὐδὲν θεῖον ἀλλὰ πονηρῶν ἐστιν ἔργα. οὕτως ὁ τοῖς Μωϋσέως ἀπιστῶν φήσει πρὸς αὐτὸν τὰ προειρημένα ἐκτιθέμενος τὸ αὐτό· ὥστε οὐδ᾿ αὐτὸς Μωϋσῆς ἔξαρνός ἐστιν, ὡς ταῦτά γε οὐδὲν θεῖον ἀλλὰ πονηρῶν ἐστιν ἔργα. τὸ αὐτὸ δὲ ποιήσει καὶ ἐπὶ τούτου· βιαζόμενος ὑπὸ τῆς ἀληθείας ὁμοῦ καὶ τὰ τῶν ἄλλων ἀπεκάλυψε καὶ τὰ καθ᾿ ἑαυτὸν ἤλεγξεν ὁ Μωϋσῆς. λέγοντι δὲ τῷ Ἰουδαίῳ καὶ τό· πῶς οὖν οὐ σχέτλιον ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ἔργων τὸν μὲν θεὸν τοὺς δὲ γόητας ἡγεῖσθαι; εἴποι τις ἂν πρὸς αὐτὸν διὰ τὰς Μωϋσέως ἐκτεθείσας λέξεις· πῶς οὖν οὐ σχέτλιον ἀπὸ τῶν αὐτῶν ἔργων τὸν μὲν προφήτην θεοῦ καὶ θεράποντα αὐτοῦ τοὺς δὲ γόητας ἡγεῖσθαι; ἐπεὶ δὲ προσδιατρίβων τῷ τόπῳ ὁ Κέλσος προσέθηκεν οἷς ἐξεθέμην κοινοποιηθεῖσι καὶ τό· τί γὰρ μᾶλλον ἀπό γε τούτων τοὺς ἄλλους πονηροὺς ἢ τοῦτον νομιστέον αὐτῷ χρωμένους μάρτυρι; προσθήσομεν τοῖς λεγομένοις καὶ ἡμεῖς τοιαῦτα· τί γὰρ μᾶλλον ἀπό γε τούτων, οἷς ἀπαγορεύει πείθεσθαι Μωϋσῆς ἐπιδεικνυμένοις σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα, ἐκείνους πονηροὺς νομιστέον ἢ Μωϋσέα ἐξ ὧν ἑτέρους περὶ σημείων καὶ τεράτων διέβαλε; πλείονα δ᾿ εἰς ταὐτὸν λέγων, ἵνα δόξῃ αὔξειν τὸ ἐπιχείρημα, φησί· ταῦτα μέν γε καὶ αὐτὸς ὡμολόγησεν οὐχὶ θείας φύσεως ἀλλ᾿ ἀπατεώνων τινῶν καὶ παμπονήρων εἶναι γνωρίσματα. τίς οὖν αὐτός; σὺ μὲν, ὦ Ἰουδαῖε. φῂς ὅτι ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ὁ δὲ ἐγκαλῶν σοι ὡς τοῖς αὐτοῖς ἐγκλήμασιν ὑποκειμένῳ τὸ αὐτὸς ἀνάξει ἐπὶ τὸν Μωϋσέα.
pass_a_gloss: And all things which the Jew in Celsus says to those believing (πιστεύω) in Jesus can be made common (κοινοποιέω) toward the accusation (κατηγορία) of Moses; so that either to say the sorcery (γοητεία) of Jesus differs in nothing from Moses' or is near-like (παραπλήσιος), both, as far as the wording (λέξις) of the Jew in Celsus goes, being able to be brought under (ὑπάγω) the same charges (ἐγκλήματα). For instance about Christ the Jew in Celsus says: 'But O light (φῶς) and truth (ἀλήθεια)! With his own voice (φωνή) Jesus expressly (διαρρήδην) declares (ἐξαγορεύω) these things, just as you also have written (συγγράφω): that others too will be present to you using like powers (δυνάμεις), wicked (κακοί) and sorcerers (γόητες).' But about Moses the one disbelieving (ἀπιστέω) Moses' things, whether an Egyptian or anyone, would say to the Jew: 'But O light and truth, with his own voice Moses expressly declares, just as you also have written, that others will be present to you using like powers, wicked and sorcerers. For it is written in your law (νόμος): if there arise among you a prophet or one dreaming a dream (ἐνυπνιαζόμενος ἐνύπνιον) and he give you a sign (σημεῖον) or wonder (τέρας), and the sign or the wonder come which he spoke to you saying: let us go and follow other gods (θεοῖς ἑτέροις) whom you do not know, and let us serve (λατρεύω) them, you shall not hear the words of that prophet or of the one dreaming that dream, and what follows.' And the one slandering (διαβάλλω) the words of Jesus says he also names (ὀνομάζω) some Satan (σατανᾶς) contriving (παραμηχανάομαι) such things; but the one making this common toward Moses will say he too names a dreaming prophet contriving such things. And as the Jew in Celsus says about Jesus that 'so that not even he himself is denying (ἔξαρνος), that these at least have nothing divine but are works (ἔργα) of wicked men (πονηροί)', so the one disbelieving Moses' things will say to him, setting out (ἐκτίθημι) the things said before, the same: 'so that not even Moses himself is denying that these at least are nothing divine but works of wicked men.' And he will do the same also with this: 'being forced (βιάζομαι) by the truth, Moses at once both uncovered (ἀποκαλύπτω) the things of the others and convicted (ἐλέγχω) his own.' And to the Jew saying also this: 'how then is it not wretched/outrageous (σχέτλιος) from the same works to regard (ἡγέομαι) the one a god, the others sorcerers?' one might say to him on account of Moses' set-out wordings: 'how then is it not outrageous from the same works to regard the one a prophet of God and his attendant/servant (θεράπων), the others sorcerers?' And since Celsus, lingering (προσδιατρίβω) on the topic (τόπος), added to the things I set out, made common, also this: 'for why from these at least must one think (νομιστέον) the others wicked rather than this one, using him himself as witness (μάρτυς)?' we too will add to the things said such as these: 'for why from these at least, those whom Moses forbids (ἀπαγορεύω) to be obeyed (πείθομαι) when displaying (ἐπιδείκνυμι) signs and wonders, must one think those wicked rather than Moses, from the things by which he slandered others about signs and wonders?' And saying more to the same, so that he may seem to increase (αὔξω) the argument (ἐπιχείρημα), he says: 'these at least he himself also agreed (ὁμολογέω) to be tokens (γνωρίσματα) not of divine nature (φύσις) but of some deceivers (ἀπατεῶνες) and utterly wicked (παμπόνηροι).' Who then is 'he himself'? You, O Jew, say that [it is] Jesus; but the one charging (ἐγκαλέω) you as subject (ὑπόκειμαι) to the same charges will refer (ἀνάγω) the 'he himself' to Moses.
pass_b_english: Indeed, everything that the Jew in Celsus says to those who believe in Jesus can be turned equally into a charge against Moses, so that one may say that the sorcery of Jesus either does not differ at all from that of Moses or is very like it, since both, as far as the words of Celsus’s Jew go, can be brought under the same charges. For example, about Christ the Jew in Celsus says: “But O light and truth! With his own voice Jesus openly declares these things, as you yourselves have recorded: that others too will come to you using like powers, wicked men and sorcerers” (compare Matthew 24:24).

But about Moses, one who disbelieves the writings of Moses, whether an Egyptian or anyone at all, might say to the Jew: ‘But O light and truth! With his own voice Moses openly declares, as you yourselves have recorded, that others will come to you using like powers, wicked men and sorcerers. For it is written in your law: “If a prophet arises among you, or one who dreams a dream, and gives you a sign or a wonder, and the sign or the wonder comes to pass of which he spoke to you, saying, Let us go and follow other gods, whom you do not know, and let us serve them, you shall not listen to the words of that prophet, or of the one who dreams that dream” (Deuteronomy 13:1–3), and so on.’

And the one who slanders the words of Jesus says that he even names a certain Satan as contriving such things; but the one who turns this against Moses will say that Moses too names a prophet who dreams dreams as contriving such things. And just as the Jew in Celsus says of Jesus: “So that not even he himself denies that these things, at least, are nothing divine, but are the works of wicked men,” so the one who disbelieves the writings of Moses will set out the passage already quoted and say the same to him: ‘So that not even Moses himself denies that these things, at least, are nothing divine, but are the works of wicked men.’ He will do the same with this too: ‘Compelled by the truth, Moses at one stroke both laid bare the deeds of others and convicted his own.’

And when the Jew also says: “How then is it not monstrous, from the same works, to think the one a god and the others sorcerers?” someone might say to him, on account of the words of Moses set out above: ‘How then is it not monstrous, from the same works, to think the one a prophet of God and his servant (Numbers 12:7), and the others sorcerers?’

And since Celsus, dwelling on this point, added this too to the words I have set out and turned against Moses: “For why, on the strength of these things at least, should we think the others wicked rather than this man, when we have him as our witness?” we too shall add something like this to what has been said: ‘For why, on the strength of these things at least, should we think those wicked whom Moses says must not be obeyed when they display signs and wonders, rather than Moses, on account of the very words by which he slandered others over signs and wonders?’

Saying more to the same effect, so as to seem to strengthen his argument, he says: “These things, at any rate, he himself admitted to be the marks not of a divine nature but of certain deceivers and utter scoundrels.” Who, then, is “he himself”? You, Jew, say that it is Jesus; but the one who accuses you, as liable to the same charges, will refer “he himself” to Moses.

choices.why: προσδιατρίβων τῷ τόπῳ: 'lingering on the passage' -> 'dwelling on this point' (τόπος = topic, not a text)
οἷς ἀπαγορεύει πείθεσθαι Μωϋσῆς: 'whom Moses forbids us to obey' -> 'whom Moses says must not be obeyed' (no added 'us')

translator_notes: Quotation marks: double quotes are Celsus’s own words (and Scripture); single quotes mark the hypothetical speeches Origen puts in the mouth of a critic of Moses, which parody Celsus’s sentences word for word. Nested Scripture inside such a speech keeps double quotes, and the innermost speech (‘Let us go...’) is left unmarked to avoid a third level. Celsus’s report of Jesus’ warning about others with like powers paraphrases Matthew 24:24 (compare Matthew 7:22–23); cited as ‘compare’ because Celsus does not quote it. Deuteronomy 13:1–3 is quoted from the LXX (LXX 13:2–4 in Rahlfs; English 13:1–3); ‘and so on’ renders καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. ‘Satan contriving such things’ repeats Celsus’s charge from 2.49 indirectly, so it is not quoted; no single verse is cited for it. ‘Prophet of God and his servant’ (θεράπων) echoes LXX Numbers 12:7. τὸν μὲν θεόν in the Jew’s mouth is rendered ‘a god’ (the speaker does not grant the claim). ‘Compelled by the truth...’ adapts Celsus’s sentence in 2.49.
